items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following integral:
[MATH: \int \cos \sqrt{x} \, \textrm dx\,]

Content:
Unfortunately, we cannot compute this integral using any of our standard methods. However, we can express this integral as an infinite series if we first write the integrand [MATH: \cos \sqrt{x}] as a Maclaurin series.

Content:
Let's start with the Maclaurin series expansion of [MATH: \cos{x},] valid for all [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \cos{x}	=1 - \frac{1}{2!}x^2 + \frac{1}{4!}x^4+\cdots \,.]

Content:
Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: \sqrt{x}] in the above equation, we find the series expansion for [MATH: \cos{\sqrt{x}}] as follows:
[MATH: \cos sqrt(x)|= 1 − (1)/(2!)(sqrt(x))^{2} + (1)/(4!)(sqrt(x))^{4} + ⋯; = 1 − (x)/(2) + (x^{2})/(24) + ⋯]

Content:
Integrating both sides of this equality, we get
[MATH: ∫\cos sqrt(x)dx|= ∫(1 − (x)/(2) + (x^{2})/(24) + ⋯)dx; = ∫1dx − (1)/(2)∫xdx + (1)/(24)∫x^{2}dx + ⋯; = C + x − (1)/(2) ⋅ (x^{2})/(2) + (1)/(24) ⋅ (x^{3})/(3) + ⋯; = C + x − (x^{2})/(4) + (x^{3})/(72) + ⋯.]

Content:
And we're done! We've just found the Maclaurin series expression for [MATH: \displaystyle \int\cos{\sqrt{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x.]

Content:
We can apply the same method to any function [MATH: f(x)] having a power series expansion of the form
[MATH: f(x)=a_0+a_1 x+a_2 x^2 + \cdots\,.]

Content:
Integrating the above, we get
[MATH: ∫f(x)dx|= ∫(a_{0} + a_{1}x + a_{2}x^{2} + ⋯)dx; = a_{0}∫dx + a_{1}∫xdx + a_{2}∫x^{2}dx + ⋯; = C + a_{0}x + a_{1}(x^{2})/(2) + a_{2}(x^{3})/(3) + ⋯.]
This is valid for the same radius of convergence as the series expansion of [MATH: f(x).]

Starting with the standard Maclaurin result for [MATH: e^x,] find the first three terms of the series expansion for [MATH: \displaystyle{\int e^{-x^2}\textrm{d}x}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The series expansion of [MATH: e^{x}] is
[MATH: e^{x}|= 1 + x + (1)/(2!)x^{2} + ⋯.]
Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: -x^2] in the above formula, we get
[MATH: e^{− x^{2}}|= 1 + (− x^{2}) + (1)/(2!)(− x^{2})^{2} + ⋯; = 1 − x^{2} + (1)/(2)x^{4} + ⋯.]
Finally, integrating with respect to [MATH: x,] we get
[MATH: ∫e^{− x^{2}}dx|= ∫(1 − x^{2} + (1)/(2)x^{4} + ⋯)dx; = C + x − (1)/(3)x^{3} + (1)/(10)x^{5} + ⋯.]

Using the standard form of the Maclaurin series of [MATH: \ln(1+x)], find the first three non-zero terms of the series expansion of the definite integral
[MATH: \displaystyle{\int_0^{1/2}\ln(1-x^2)\text{d}x}.]

sections.normalized_html:
The power series expansion of [MATH: \ln(1+x)] is given by [MATH: \ln (1 + x) = x − (1)/(2)x^{2} + (1)/(3)x^{3} + ⋯.]

Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: -x^2] in the above, we get [MATH: \ln (1 − x^{2})|= (− x^{2}) − (1)/(2)(− x^{2})^{2} + (1)/(3)(− x^{2})^{3} + ⋯; = − x^{2} − (1)/(2)x^{4} − (1)/(3)x^{6} + ⋯.]

Finally, we calculate the definite integral, as follows: [MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|= ∫(− x^{2} − (1)/(2)x^{4} − (1)/(3)x^{6} + ⋯)dx; = (− (x^{3})/(3) − (1)/(2) ⋅ (x^{5})/(5) − (1)/(3) ⋅ (x^{7})/(7) + ⋯)|_{0}^{1/2}; = − (1)/(3 ⋅ 2^{3}) − (1)/(2 ⋅ 5 ⋅ 2^{5}) − (1)/(3 ⋅ 7 ⋅ 2^{7}); = − (1)/(24) − (1)/(320) − (1)/(2688) + ⋯]

Note: We can get a numerical approximation by evaluating the first three terms. This gives

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|≈ − (1)/(24) − (1)/(320) − (1)/(2688) = − 0.04516]

rounded to five decimal places.

The exact value of the integral, rounded to five decimal places, is [MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|= − 0.04523.] So, our estimation was pretty good!

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the following integral:
[MATH: \int \cos \sqrt{x} \, \textrm dx\,]

Content:
Unfortunately, we cannot compute this integral using any of our standard methods. However, we can express this integral as an infinite series if we first write the integrand [MATH: \cos \sqrt{x}] as a Maclaurin series.

Content:
Let's start with the Maclaurin series expansion of [MATH: \cos{x},] valid for all [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \cos{x}	=1 - \frac{1}{2!}x^2 + \frac{1}{4!}x^4+\cdots \,.]

Content:
Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: \sqrt{x}] in the above equation, we find the series expansion for [MATH: \cos{\sqrt{x}}] as follows:
[MATH: \cos sqrt(x)|= 1 − (1)/(2!)(sqrt(x))^{2} + (1)/(4!)(sqrt(x))^{4} + ⋯; = 1 − (x)/(2) + (x^{2})/(24) + ⋯]

Content:
Integrating both sides of this equality, we get
[MATH: ∫\cos sqrt(x)dx|= ∫(1 − (x)/(2) + (x^{2})/(24) + ⋯)dx; = ∫1dx − (1)/(2)∫xdx + (1)/(24)∫x^{2}dx + ⋯; = C + x − (1)/(2) ⋅ (x^{2})/(2) + (1)/(24) ⋅ (x^{3})/(3) + ⋯; = C + x − (x^{2})/(4) + (x^{3})/(72) + ⋯.]

Content:
And we're done! We've just found the Maclaurin series expression for [MATH: \displaystyle \int\cos{\sqrt{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x.]

Content:
We can apply the same method to any function [MATH: f(x)] having a power series expansion of the form
[MATH: f(x)=a_0+a_1 x+a_2 x^2 + \cdots\,.]

Content:
Integrating the above, we get
[MATH: ∫f(x)dx|= ∫(a_{0} + a_{1}x + a_{2}x^{2} + ⋯)dx; = a_{0}∫dx + a_{1}∫xdx + a_{2}∫x^{2}dx + ⋯; = C + a_{0}x + a_{1}(x^{2})/(2) + a_{2}(x^{3})/(3) + ⋯.]
This is valid for the same radius of convergence as the series expansion of [MATH: f(x).]

Item 5 — Example: Computing Definite Integrals Using Taylor Series

Example Prompt:
Using the standard form of the Maclaurin series of [MATH: \ln(1+x)], find the first three non-zero terms of the series expansion of the definite integral
[MATH: \displaystyle{\int_0^{1/2}\ln(1-x^2)\text{d}x}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The power series expansion of [MATH: \ln(1+x)] is given by
[MATH: \ln (1 + x) = x − (1)/(2)x^{2} + (1)/(3)x^{3} + ⋯.]

Replacing [MATH: x] with [MATH: -x^2] in the above, we get
[MATH: \ln (1 − x^{2})|= (− x^{2}) − (1)/(2)(− x^{2})^{2} + (1)/(3)(− x^{2})^{3} + ⋯; = − x^{2} − (1)/(2)x^{4} − (1)/(3)x^{6} + ⋯.]

Finally, we calculate the definite integral, as follows:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|= ∫(− x^{2} − (1)/(2)x^{4} − (1)/(3)x^{6} + ⋯)dx; = (− (x^{3})/(3) − (1)/(2) ⋅ (x^{5})/(5) − (1)/(3) ⋅ (x^{7})/(7) + ⋯)|_{0}^{1/2}; = − (1)/(3 ⋅ 2^{3}) − (1)/(2 ⋅ 5 ⋅ 2^{5}) − (1)/(3 ⋅ 7 ⋅ 2^{7}); = − (1)/(24) − (1)/(320) − (1)/(2688) + ⋯]

Note: We can get a numerical approximation by evaluating the first three terms. This gives

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|≈ − (1)/(24) − (1)/(320) − (1)/(2688) = − 0.04516]

rounded to five decimal places.

The exact value of the integral, rounded to five decimal places, is
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1/2}\ln (1 − x^{2})dx|= − 0.04523.]
So, our estimation was pretty good!
